title: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
summary: Why C pointer bugs compile and ship, how Rust's pointer types turn them into compile errors or panics, what unsafe really unlocks, how to build sound safe wrappers, and how to cross into C via FFI.
outcomes: Explain why use after free and out-of-bounds bugs compile cleanly in C and how Rust reports the same code
Map C pointer roles to Box, &T, &mut T, slices and raw pointers, and say what each guarantees
List the five operations unsafe unlocks and explain why it does not disable the borrow checker
Judge whether an unsafe-backed function is sound, using split_at_mut and module privacy as models
Write an FFI call that keeps ownership and layout correct with CString and #[repr(C)]

lessons.title: Why C memory bugs compile cleanly and ship

blocks.md:
You already know the Rust side: one owner per value, drop at end of scope, many readers or one writer. This course puts that next to C, the language most systems code is still written in, and then opens the escape hatch Rust keeps for the cases its checker cannot prove: `unsafe`.

In C a pointer is just an address. The type `char *` says nothing about whether the holder must call `free`, whether the block is still alive, or how many bytes it covers. The compiler checks none of that.

blocks.caption: Compiles with no warnings under clang -Wall -Wextra. Line 12 reads freed memory.

blocks.title: Use after free: a stale pointer reads someone else's data

scenes.caption: `malloc(8)` returns block A and `name` holds its address. Nothing in the program records that `name` is responsible for freeing it. Simplified: allocator metadata is not shown.
`strcpy` writes the 5 letters of alice plus the terminating zero byte into block A.
`alias = name` copies the address. Both pointers look identical to the compiler; neither is marked as the owner.
`free(name)` hands block A back to the allocator. Nothing erases it (simplified: the allocator may write bookkeeping into it) and both variables still hold address A, but both are now dangling.
The next `malloc(8)` of the same size got block A back in our -O0 run on macOS. Reuse is up to the allocator, which is why the bug is intermittent.
`strcpy(other, "mallory")` overwrites the block with 7 letters and a zero byte. The new owner did nothing wrong.
`printf("%s", alias)` reads through the stale pointer and prints mallory: data that belongs to another part of the program. In an attacker's hands this is a read or write primitive.

blocks.prompt: What does this program print? Think about it before revealing: the C standard calls line 12 undefined behavior.
blocks.reveal:
It depends, which is exactly the problem. On our macOS test machine an unoptimized build (-O0) printed **mallory**, the next owner's data. The same source built with -O2 printed **a single garbage byte** (0x02, so the line looked empty). Built with AddressSanitizer (`-fsanitize=address`), it stopped with `heap-use-after-free` at line 12 and also reported where the block was freed (line 9) and allocated (line 6).

**Undefined behavior** (UB) means the language standard places no requirement on what happens, so the optimizer may assume it never occurs. The program is not "slightly wrong"; it has no meaning.

blocks.md:
The same root cause, a pointer whose validity nobody tracks, produces a family of bugs:

- **Use after free**: reading or writing a block after `free`.
- **Double free**: calling `free` twice, which corrupts allocator state.
- **Out of bounds**: indexing past the end, because a pointer does not carry a length.
- **Uninitialized read**: using bytes nothing wrote.
- **Data race**: two threads touching the same memory, at least one writing, with no synchronization.

blocks.title: Share of security bugs that are memory safety bugs

scenes.caption: Chromium: around 70% of high and critical severity security bugs (912 bugs since 2015) are memory unsafety, and half of those are use after free, so roughly 35%.
Android: memory safety bugs were 76% of its vulnerabilities in 2019, in line with the roughly 70% industry norm the Android team cites.
After new Android code moved mostly to memory safe languages (Rust, Java, Kotlin), the share fell to 24% in 2024, even though most existing code is still C and C++.

blocks.md: Tools such as AddressSanitizer and fuzzing find many of these bugs, but only on inputs that actually run. The Android team describes them as treating symptoms rather than the root cause, and notes that coverage stays low without constant pressure on teams to fuzz and triage.
C's type system cannot express *who owns this block* or *how long this pointer is valid*. Rust's ownership and borrow rules are exactly that missing information, checked at compile time.

blocks.question: A C function returns `char *`. What does its type tell the caller about freeing the result?
options: The caller must free it, because it is a non-const pointer
Nothing: ownership is only in the documentation, the compiler cannot check it
The function frees it when the caller returns
It must be freed with the allocator that matches its type
blocks.explain: A raw C pointer carries no ownership or lifetime information. Whether the caller must call `free`, must not, or must call a library specific function is a convention written in docs. That gap is what makes leaks, double frees and use after free easy to write.

blocks.question: The Android team kept most of its existing C and C++ code but wrote new code in memory safe languages. What happened to the memory safety share of its vulnerabilities between 2019 and 2024?
options: It stayed near 70%, because old code still dominates
It rose, because FFI glue introduced new bugs
It fell from 76% to 24%
It fell to 0%, because Rust code has no unsafe
blocks.explain: The September 2024 Google Security Blog post reports 76% in 2019 and 24% in 2024. Their explanation: most vulnerabilities live in new or recently changed code, and vulnerability density decays as code ages, so stopping the inflow of new unsafe code pays off quickly.

lessons.title: The same bugs in Rust: compile errors, panics, and what slips through

blocks.md: Rust splits C's single `T *` into several pointer types, each carrying the information C leaves in comments. Recall from the prerequisite: a borrow (`&T` or `&mut T`) may not outlive its owner, and you can have many `&T` or one `&mut T`, never both.

blocks.title: One C pointer type, five Rust pointer types

scenes.caption: In C all five of these are spelled `T *` (plus maybe `const`). The meaning lives in comments and conventions.
An owning heap pointer becomes `Box<T>`: exactly one owner, and the drop at end of scope is the only `free`. Double free cannot be written in safe code.
Read-only and read-write arguments become `&T` and `&mut T`. The borrow checker proves they never outlive the owner and that a `&mut` is never aliased.
Pointer plus separate length becomes a slice, a fat pointer that stores both. Every `s[i]` is bounds checked against that length.
Anything the compiler cannot reason about stays a raw pointer, which behaves like C's. Creating one is safe; dereferencing one requires `unsafe` (next lesson).

blocks.md: Here is lesson 1's use after free, translated. `drop(name)` is Rust's explicit way to end ownership early; it is a move, so the compiler checks it against outstanding borrows.

blocks.caption: Real rustc output, abbreviated. The bug is reported at compile time with all three lines that form it.

blocks.md: Not every bug can be ruled out before the program runs. An index computed from input is the classic case. Rust's answer is a **run-time check** that turns undefined behavior into a defined failure: a **panic**, which unwinds the thread (or aborts) with a message.

blocks.title: An index the compiler cannot know: Rust checks it at run time

scenes.caption: `v` is a `Vec<i32>`: pointer, length 3, capacity 3. The length travels with the pointer.
The index comes from run-time input (argument count 1, plus 4), so no compile-time check can catch it.
`v[i]` compares 5 against the stored length 3 before touching memory and panics. The process exits with status 101 instead of reading past the buffer.
scenes.output:
thread 'main' panicked at oob.rs:4:21:
index out of bounds: the len is 3 but the index is 5

blocks.prompt: The C version (`int v[3]`, `printf("%d", v[argc + 4])`) compiled with one unrelated warning. What did it print?
blocks.reveal: An arbitrary integer: whatever 4 bytes happened to sit 8 bytes past the end of the array (on our run, 911781002), and it exited with status 0 as if nothing went wrong. Silent wrong answers are worse than crashes, because nothing tells you to look.

blocks.title: Pointer sizes on a 64-bit target (bytes, rustc measured)

scenes.caption: A reference, a Box and a raw pointer are each one 8-byte address. A slice reference is 16 bytes: address plus length. That length is what makes bounds checks possible.
`Option<Box<u8>>` is still 8 bytes: Box is never null, so None is stored as the null address. `Option<*const u8>` needs 16 bytes, because a raw pointer may already be null.

blocks.md:
Safe Rust's promise is narrower than "no bugs". It rules out undefined behavior: no use after free, no double free, no out-of-bounds access, no data races. These remain possible and are considered memory safe:

- **Leaks**: `Rc` cycles or `Box::leak` keep memory alive forever. The Rust Book states that preventing leaks is not one of Rust's guarantees.
- **Panics**: a failed bounds check is a crash, just a defined one.
- **Integer overflow**: debug builds panic; release builds wrap in two's complement (255u8 + 1 becomes 0) unless you use `checked_*` or `wrapping_*` methods.
- **Logic bugs and deadlocks**.

Misconception: "Rust has no runtime checks, everything is proven at compile time." Lifetimes and aliasing are checked at compile time; indexing, `RefCell` borrows and debug-mode overflow are checked at run time. The design goal is that every remaining failure is defined, not that there are none.

blocks.question: Which bug does safe Rust still allow, by design?
options: Reading an element past the end of a `Vec`
Two threads writing the same `i32` without a lock
A leak from two `Rc` values that point at each other
Using a `String` after it has been dropped
blocks.explain: Out-of-bounds access becomes a panic, sharing mutable data across threads without a lock or atomic fails to compile, and use after drop is a borrow error. Leaks are explicitly memory safe in Rust: an `Rc` cycle never reaches count 0, so its memory is never freed.

blocks.question: Why can `Option<&T>` be passed to C as a plain nullable pointer, but `Option<*const T>` cannot?
options: A reference is never null, so None can use the null address and the Option stays one pointer wide
References are always 16 bytes
C cannot read Rust enums of any kind
Raw pointers are not allowed inside Option
blocks.explain: The std `Option` docs guarantee that `Option<&T>`, `Option<&mut T>`, `Option<Box<T>>` and `Option<NonNull<T>>` have the same size, alignment and ABI as the inner pointer, with None as null. A raw pointer can already be null, so Option needs a separate tag (we measured 16 bytes).

lessons.title: unsafe: five extra powers, same borrow checker

blocks.md: Static analysis is conservative: the compiler would rather reject a correct program than accept a wrong one. And the hardware itself (device registers, system calls, C libraries) knows nothing about ownership. So Rust contains a second language, **unsafe Rust**, entered with the `unsafe` keyword.

The Rust Book lists exactly five things an `unsafe` block or function allows that safe Rust does not:

1. Dereference a raw pointer (`*const T`, `*mut T`).
2. Call an `unsafe` function or method.
3. Access or modify a mutable `static` variable.
4. Implement an `unsafe` trait (such as `Send` or `Sync`).
5. Access fields of a `union`.

Misconception: "`unsafe` turns off the borrow checker." It does not. References inside an unsafe block are checked exactly as before: two `&mut x` in an `unsafe` block still fail with E0499 (rustc also warns that the block is unnecessary). `unsafe` only unlocks the five operations above.

Raw pointers are the C pointers of Rust. Unlike references, they may alias freely (several `*mut T` to one place), may be null, may dangle, and never free anything on their own. The new `&raw const x` and `&raw mut x` operators create them directly.

blocks.caption: Prints 7. Without the unsafe block, `*a += 1` is error E0133: dereference of raw pointer is unsafe and requires unsafe function or block.

blocks.title: Raw pointers: two writers to one place, and a wild address

scenes.caption: `let mut x = 5`. Two `&mut x` at once would be rejected with E0499, even inside an unsafe block.
`&raw mut x` twice gives two `*mut i32` aimed at x. Raw pointers ignore the borrowing rules, and creating them needs no unsafe.
`*a += 1` inside `unsafe`: you, not the compiler, vouch that a points to a live, aligned i32 and that no reference to x is in use.
`*b += 1` writes through the second pointer. Single-threaded and with no live references, this is fine; the program prints 7.
Casting the integer 0x12345 to `*const i32` is also safe. Dereferencing it is undefined behavior: there may be nothing mapped there, or the optimizer may delete the access.

blocks.md: An **unsafe function** is one with a precondition the compiler cannot check, written as `unsafe fn`. Calling it requires an `unsafe` block, which is your signature that you read the contract and meet it. Standard example: `Vec::set_len(n)` is unsafe because it requires `n <= capacity()` and that the elements up to `n` are initialized; break either and later reads touch garbage.

blocks.caption: Idiom from the Rust Book: an unsafe fn documents its contract, and every unsafe block says in a SAFETY comment why the contract holds.

blocks.md:
What exactly must you avoid? The Rust Reference keeps a list of **behavior considered undefined**, which applies to unsafe code too. Highlights:

- Data races.
- Accessing memory through a dangling or misaligned pointer.
- Breaking the aliasing rules: memory behind a live `&T` must not be mutated (outside `UnsafeCell`), and a live `&mut T` must be the only way to reach its memory.
- Producing an invalid value, for example a `bool` that is not 0 or 1, or a null reference.

The Reference warns the list is not exhaustive.

`unsafe` does not change the rules; it changes who checks them. Rust programs must never cause undefined behavior, inside or outside unsafe blocks. Inside, the proof obligation moves from the compiler to you.

blocks.question: Which line needs an `unsafe` block?
options: `let p = 0x1000usize as *const u8;`
`let n = v.len();` on a `Vec<u8>`
`v.set_len(4);` on a `Vec<u8>`
`let r = &raw const x;`
blocks.explain: Creating raw pointers (by cast or with `&raw`) is safe: nothing happens until you dereference. `set_len` is an `unsafe fn` because it trusts you that the new length is within capacity and the elements are initialized, so calling it needs an unsafe block.

blocks.question: A teammate wraps a function body in `unsafe { ... }` to silence E0502 (a shared and a mutable borrow overlap). What happens?
options: It compiles, because unsafe disables borrow checking in the block
It still fails with E0502; unsafe does not relax the borrow rules on references
It compiles but inserts a run-time borrow check
It compiles only in release mode
blocks.explain: The Book is explicit: unsafe does not turn off the borrow checker or other safety checks on references. To express aliasing the checker cannot verify, you must switch to raw pointers (or `UnsafeCell` based types) and take responsibility for the rules yourself.

lessons.title: Safe wrappers over unsafe code: split_at_mut and soundness

blocks.md: Most unsafe code exists to build a **safe abstraction**: a function or type with a safe API whose implementation uses a few unsafe operations the checker cannot verify. `Vec`, `String`, `split_at_mut` and the standard library's locks all work this way.

The Rust Book's example: split one mutable slice into two mutable halves. The obvious safe version, `(&mut values[..mid], &mut values[mid..])`, is rejected with E0499 (cannot borrow `*values` as mutable more than once). The checker sees two `&mut` borrows of the same slice; it does not reason that the index ranges are disjoint.

blocks.caption: Rust Book Listing 20-6. The function is not marked unsafe, so any safe code may call it.

blocks.title: split_at_mut: two disjoint mutable halves from one pointer

scenes.caption: `v = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]`, len 6. Cells 6 to 9 are memory past the buffer that v does not own.
`as_mut_ptr()` yields a `*mut i32` to element 0. `assert!(mid <= len)` checks 3 <= 6 before any unsafe code runs.
`from_raw_parts_mut(ptr, 3)` builds the left slice over indices 0 to 2.
`ptr.add(3)` and length 6 - 3 = 3 build the right slice over indices 3 to 5. The two ranges do not overlap, so two `&mut` are sound.
Callers use them like any slices: `left[0] = 10; right[0] = 40;` leaves v as [10, 2, 3, 40, 5, 6]. The caller never wrote unsafe.

Delete the assert and call with mid = 8 in a release build: left claims 8 elements (2 past the end) and right starts at index 8 with length 6 - 8 wrapped to 18446744073709551614. Both slices are invalid: undefined behavior.

blocks.prompt: Remove `assert!(mid <= len)` and call `split_at_mut(&mut v, 8)` on the 6-element vector. What happens in a debug build versus a release build?
blocks.reveal:
**Debug:** the subtraction `len - mid` is `6 - 8` on `usize`, which panics with *attempt to subtract with overflow*. Luck, not design: the overflow check fired before the bad slice was used.

**Release (-O):** overflow checks are off, so `6 - 8` wraps to 18446744073709551614. Our run printed `8 18446744073709551614` as the two lengths. Both slices point at memory v does not own. That is undefined behavior reachable from safe code, which makes the function **unsound**.

blocks.md: The Rust Reference defines the bar: unsafe code is **sound** if no safe code that calls it can trigger undefined behavior; otherwise it is **unsound**. The `assert!` is not decoration. It is the proof that every pointer built inside the unsafe block stays in bounds.

blocks.title: One safe-code edit makes the unsafe block unsound

scenes.caption: Example from the Rustonomicon. With the original `<`, index(4) fails the test 4 < 4 and returns None, so the unchecked read only runs for idx 0 to 3: sound.
Someone edits only the safe comparison to `<=`. Now 4 <= 4 is true and control enters the unsafe block.
`get_unchecked(4)` reads one byte past the array: undefined behavior. A debug build caught it with a standard library precondition check; an optimized build on our machine died on a trap instruction.
scenes.output:
thread 'main' panicked at idx.rs:3:28:
unsafe precondition(s) violated: slice::get_unchecked requires that the index is within the slice

blocks.md:
The lesson from that example is that safety is **non-local**: the unsafe block's correctness depends on state set up by ordinary safe code around it. The Rustonomicon makes the same point with a hand-written `Vec { ptr, len, cap }`: `push` writes at `ptr.add(len)` assuming `cap` matches the allocation. A 100% safe private method that does `self.cap += 1` breaks that assumption.

The fix is **privacy**. If `cap` is a private field, only code in the same module can touch it, so the audit boundary is the module, not the whole program.

Audit unsafe code at the module boundary. Keep fields that unsafe code trusts private, check every invariant before the unsafe block (as `assert!(mid <= len)` does), and write a SAFETY comment that names the invariant.

**Miri** is the official tool for finding undefined behavior in unsafe code. It interprets your program or test suite and flags violations such as dangling pointers, out-of-bounds access and aliasing rule breaks. It needs the nightly toolchain (`rustup +nightly component add miri`, then `cargo +nightly miri test`).

A clean Miri run is evidence, not proof. Miri is dynamic: it only checks the paths your tests execute, and the Book notes it does not cover every way code can be unsound. Combine it with tests that hit the edge cases, such as mid = len and mid = len + 1.

blocks.question: Which change can make a sound module containing a hand-written `Vec` unsound, without touching any unsafe block?
options: Adding a private method that returns `self.len`
Adding a `pub fn set_cap(&mut self, c: usize)` that assigns `self.cap = c`
Renaming the `push` method
Adding a test that pushes 1000 elements
blocks.explain: The unsafe code in `push` trusts `cap` to match the real allocation. A public setter lets any safe caller break that invariant and make `push` write out of bounds. Reading `len` cannot break anything, and tests do not change the code's soundness.

blocks.question: Your unsafe-backed parser passes `cargo miri test` with no errors. What can you conclude?
options: The parser can never cause undefined behavior
The inputs your tests ran did not trigger any UB that Miri detects
The parser is safe to mark `Sync`
The borrow checker has verified the unsafe blocks
blocks.explain: Miri checks the executions it actually performs. Untested inputs, and kinds of unsoundness Miri does not model, can still hide bugs. It raises confidence; it does not prove soundness.

lessons.title: FFI: calling C from Rust without losing track of ownership

blocks.md: A **foreign function interface** (FFI) lets code in one language call functions in another. Rust declares C functions in an `unsafe extern "C"` block. The `"C"` names the **ABI** (application binary interface): how arguments travel in registers and on the stack. Every function in that block is unsafe to call (unless you mark it `safe`, a promise the compiler cannot check), because C enforces none of Rust's rules.

blocks.caption: Runs and prints 5, then "handoff". The only unsafe lines are the two calls whose contracts the comments explain.

blocks.md: Two ownership patterns appear here. **Borrowing across the boundary**: `as_ptr()` gives C a pointer while Rust keeps ownership, so the CString must outlive the call. **Transferring across the boundary**: `into_raw()` hands the buffer to C, and only `CString::from_raw` on that same pointer may free it. Rule of thumb from the CString docs: memory goes back to the allocator that produced it, so a buffer allocated by a C library is freed with that library's free function, never with `CString::from_raw`.

blocks.title: Who owns the bytes as a string crosses into C

scenes.caption: `CString::new("hello")` copies the text into a fresh heap buffer and appends a NUL byte (6 bytes). It fails if the text already contains a NUL.
`as_ptr()` lends C a read-only pointer. Rust still owns the buffer; the pointer is only valid while `owned` is alive.
C walks bytes until the NUL and returns 5. Nothing was transferred.
A second CString, "handoff" (8 bytes with its NUL), is made and `into_raw()` consumes it: Rust gives up ownership and will not free the buffer. Forgetting to take it back is a leak.
Wrong: calling C's `free()` on it. The CString docs forbid this; the buffer came from Rust's allocator, which need not be C's malloc.
Right: the pointer returns and `CString::from_raw` retakes ownership exactly once. When `back` is dropped, Rust's allocator frees it.

blocks.question: This compiles with no unsafe on the first line: `let p = CString::new("Hi").unwrap().as_ptr();` then later `unsafe { strlen(p) }`. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, `as_ptr` keeps the string alive
`CString::new` must be in an unsafe block
`strlen` needs `*mut c_char`, so it fails to compile
The temporary CString is dropped at the end of the first statement, so `p` dangles and `strlen(p)` is undefined behavior
blocks.explain: A raw pointer carries no lifetime, so the borrow checker cannot connect `p` to the temporary. The CStr docs use this exact example as a warning. Bind the CString to a variable that lives past the call, as `c_len` does.

blocks.md: Types that cross the boundary need a layout both sides agree on. Rust's default layout makes almost no promises, so structs shared with C are marked `#[repr(C)]`, which uses C's ordering and padding rules.

blocks.title: struct { u8 flag; u32 id; u16 port; } in memory

scenes.caption: `#[repr(C)]` follows C's rule: fields in declaration order, each at the next multiple of its alignment. flag at 0, id at 4, port at 8; size 12, of which 5 bytes are padding. clang gives the identical layout.
Default Rust layout only promises non-overlapping fields; the order is up to the compiler. rustc 1.90 put id at 0, port at 4, flag at 6: size 8. Never pass such a struct to C.

blocks.md:
Pointers that C may set to NULL map neatly onto `Option`: the std docs guarantee `Option<&T>`, `Option<Box<T>>`, `Option<NonNull<T>>` and `Option<extern "C" fn(..)>` use null for None and have the pointer's ABI, so a nullable callback can be declared without any transmute.

Going the other way, `#[unsafe(no_mangle)] pub extern "C" fn name()` exports a Rust function under a plain symbol name that C can link against.

Undefined behavior does not stay on its side of the boundary. The Rust Reference notes that UB in a called C function makes the whole program undefined, including the Rust parts, and vice versa. FFI bindings are where most real-world unsafe Rust lives, so keep them thin and wrap them in a safe API.

Typical shape of a good binding: a private `extern` block with the raw C signatures, then a public safe wrapper per function that converts types (`&str` to `CString`, null to `None`), checks the C contract, and owns any resource in a struct whose `Drop` calls the C library's free function.

blocks.question: A C library returns `char *` from `lib_get_name()` and documents that callers must release it with `lib_free_name()`. How should the Rust wrapper free it?
options: Call `lib_free_name` (for example from a `Drop` impl) after copying the bytes out
Wrap it with `CString::from_raw` and let Rust drop it
Call `libc::free`, since all C strings come from malloc
Leave it: Rust frees foreign memory automatically at scope end
blocks.explain: `CString::from_raw` is only for pointers produced by `CString::into_raw`; on foreign memory it risks allocator corruption. The library may not use malloc at all, so its own release function is the only correct one. Rust never frees memory it does not own.

blocks.question: Using C's layout rules, what is `sizeof` of `struct { uint8_t flag; uint32_t id; uint16_t port; }` on a typical 64-bit target?
options: 7 bytes, the sum of the fields
8 bytes
12 bytes
16 bytes
blocks.explain: flag sits at offset 0, then 3 padding bytes so `id` (alignment 4) starts at 4, `port` follows at 8 and ends at 10, and the total rounds up to the struct alignment 4: 12 bytes. Rust's default layout reordered the same fields into 8 bytes, which is why FFI structs need `#[repr(C)]`.
